cards.front: What does atrial fibrillation look like on ECG, and what are its common causes?
cards.back: An **irregularly irregular** rhythm with **no discrete P waves** (a wavy, fibrillatory baseline) and usually narrow QRS complexes. Common causes: **hypertension**, **mitral valve disease** (large left atrium), **hyperthyroidism**, **alcohol**, ischemic heart disease.
cards.back_pt: Ritmo **irregularmente irregular**, **sem ondas P definidas** (linha de base ondulada, fibrilatória) e QRS geralmente estreito. Causas comuns: **hipertensão**, **valvopatia mitral** (átrio esquerdo aumentado), **hipertireoidismo**, **álcool**, cardiopatia isquêmica.

cards.front: Why does atrial fibrillation cause stroke, and how is this risk reduced?
cards.back: The atria quiver instead of contracting, so blood **stagnates**, mainly in the **left atrial appendage**, and a **thrombus** forms. It can embolize to the brain (**cardioembolic stroke**). The decision to start **anticoagulation** is guided by a stroke-risk score such as **CHA2DS2-VASc**.
cards.back_pt: Os átrios fibrilam em vez de contrair, então o sangue fica **estagnado**, principalmente no **apêndice atrial esquerdo**, e forma-se um **trombo**. Ele pode embolizar para o cérebro (**AVC cardioembólico**). A decisão de iniciar **anticoagulação** é guiada por um escore de risco como o **CHA2DS2-VASc**.

cards.front: What are the ECG findings and the mechanism of typical atrial flutter?
cards.back: **Sawtooth flutter waves** (best seen in II, III, aVF) at an atrial rate near **300/min**, often with **2:1 conduction** (ventricular rate about 150/min). Mechanism: **macroreentry** around the tricuspid annulus through the **cavotricuspid isthmus**, a target for catheter ablation.
cards.back_pt: **Ondas F em dente de serra** (melhor vistas em DII, DIII, aVF) com frequência atrial perto de **300/min**, muitas vezes com **condução 2:1** (frequência ventricular de cerca de 150/min). Mecanismo: **macrorreentrada** ao redor do anel tricúspide, passando pelo **istmo cavotricuspídeo**, alvo da ablação por cateter.

cards.front: In stable AV nodal reentrant tachycardia, which drug is first-line after vagal maneuvers, and how does it stop the rhythm?
cards.back: **Adenosine**. It activates **A1 receptors** in the AV node, which opens **K+ channels** (hyperpolarization) and lowers Ca2+ entry. The result is a brief **AV block** that breaks the **reentry circuit**. Its effect lasts only seconds.
cards.back_pt: **Adenosina**. Ela ativa **receptores A1** no nó AV, o que abre **canais de K+** (hiperpolarização) e reduz a entrada de Ca2+. O resultado é um **bloqueio AV** breve que interrompe o **circuito de reentrada**. O efeito dura apenas segundos.

cards.front: What causes the ECG pattern of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome?
cards.back: An **accessory pathway** (**bundle of Kent**) bypasses the AV node and **pre-excites** part of the ventricle. ECG: **short PR**, a **delta wave** (slurred QRS upstroke) and a **wide QRS**. It predisposes to reentrant SVT.
cards.back_pt: Uma **via acessória** (**feixe de Kent**) contorna o nó AV e **pré-excita** parte do ventrículo. ECG: **PR curto**, **onda delta** (empastamento inicial do QRS) e **QRS alargado**. Predispõe a TSV por reentrada.

cards.front: How do Mobitz I and Mobitz II second-degree AV block differ?
cards.back: **Mobitz I (Wenckebach)**: PR **lengthens progressively** until a QRS drops; block usually in the **AV node**; often benign. **Mobitz II**: **constant PR**, sudden dropped QRS; block **below the AV node**; may progress to **complete block**; needs a **pacemaker**.
cards.back_pt: **Mobitz I (Wenckebach)**: o PR **aumenta progressivamente** até um QRS falhar; bloqueio geralmente no **nó AV**; costuma ser benigno. **Mobitz II**: **PR constante**, falha súbita do QRS; bloqueio **abaixo do nó AV**; pode evoluir para **BAV total**; indica-se **marca-passo**.

cards.front: How do the two classic congenital long QT syndromes differ?
cards.back: **Romano-Ward**: **autosomal dominant**, normal hearing. **Jervell and Lange-Nielsen**: **autosomal recessive**, with **congenital sensorineural deafness**. Most cases come from **K+ channel** mutations (a few Romano-Ward cases involve the Na+ channel); both carry a risk of **torsades de pointes** and sudden death.
cards.back_pt: **Romano-Ward**: **autossômica dominante**, audição normal. **Jervell e Lange-Nielsen**: **autossômica recessiva**, com **surdez neurossensorial congênita**. A maioria decorre de mutações em **canais de K+** (alguns casos de Romano-Ward envolvem o canal de Na+); ambas trazem risco de **torsades de pointes** e morte súbita.

cards.front: What are the key features of Brugada syndrome?
cards.back: Usually **autosomal dominant** loss of function of a cardiac **Na+ channel**; more common in **Asian men**. ECG: **pseudo-right bundle branch block** with **ST elevation in V1-V3**. Risk of **ventricular fibrillation** and sudden death; an **ICD** prevents sudden death.
cards.back_pt: Geralmente **autossômica dominante**, com perda de função de um **canal de Na+** cardíaco; mais comum em **homens asiáticos**. ECG: **padrão de pseudobloqueio de ramo direito** com **supradesnivelamento do ST em V1-V3**. Risco de **FV** e morte súbita; o **CDI** previne a morte súbita.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman comes to the clinic with 2 months of palpitations, weight loss, heat intolerance and a fine tremor. Pulse is about 130/min and irregular. Exam shows a diffusely enlarged, non-tender thyroid gland. TSH is very low. ECG shows narrow QRS complexes at completely irregular intervals. No clear P waves are seen; the baseline between QRS complexes is wavy and chaotic. Which rhythm is most likely?
choices: Sinus tachycardia with frequent premature atrial contractions
questions.explanation: An **irregularly irregular** narrow-complex rhythm with **no discrete P waves** is **atrial fibrillation**, and **hyperthyroidism** is a classic cause. Multifocal atrial tachycardia is also irregular, but it shows clear P waves with at least three different shapes. Atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 conduction is regular and shows sawtooth flutter waves.
questions.explanation_pt: Um ritmo de QRS estreito **irregularmente irregular**, **sem ondas P definidas**, é **FA**, e o **hipertireoidismo** é uma causa clássica. A taquicardia atrial multifocal também é irregular, mas tem ondas P nítidas com pelo menos três morfologias diferentes. O flutter atrial com condução 2:1 fixa é regular e mostra ondas F em dente de serra.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman is in the hospital with community-acquired pneumonia. She also takes furosemide for heart failure. On day 3 of a new antibiotic she faints in bed. Telemetry shows a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in which the QRS amplitude rises and falls, as if twisting around the baseline. It stops on its own. Her ECG between episodes shows a prolonged QT interval that was normal on admission. Serum potassium is 3.2 mEq/L. Which antibiotic most likely contributed to this arrhythmia?
questions.explanation: This is **torsades de pointes** caused by an **acquired long QT**. **Macrolides** such as erythromycin block cardiac K+ channels and prolong the QT, and her **hypokalemia** from furosemide adds to the risk; hypomagnesemia does the same. The other antibiotics do not typically prolong the QT. The acute treatment of torsades is **IV magnesium sulfate**, plus stopping the drug and correcting electrolytes.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se de **torsades de pointes** por **QT longo adquirido**. Os **macrolídeos**, como a eritromicina, bloqueiam canais de K+ cardíacos e prolongam o QT, e a **hipocalemia** causada pela furosemida aumenta o risco; a hipomagnesemia tem o mesmo efeito. Os outros antibióticos não costumam prolongar o QT. O tratamento agudo da torsades é **sulfato de magnésio IV**, além de suspender o fármaco e corrigir os eletrólitos.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the emergency department with sudden palpitations. Blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. ECG shows a very fast, irregularly irregular rhythm at about 240/min with wide QRS complexes that vary in width from beat to beat. An old ECG showed a short PR interval and a slurred upstroke of the QRS. He is given IV verapamil. Minutes later the ventricular rate rises further and the rhythm degenerates into ventricular fibrillation. Which mechanism best explains this deterioration?
choices: Prolongation of the QT interval leading to torsades de pointes
Block of the AV node, so more atrial impulses reach the ventricles through the accessory pathway
Coronary artery vasospasm causing acute myocardial ischemia
Increased vagal tone slowing conduction in the accessory pathway
Hyperkalemia caused by calcium channel blockade
questions.explanation: This is **atrial fibrillation with pre-excitation** in **Wolff-Parkinson-White**. Blocking the **AV node** removes the competing normal route, so the fast atrial impulses travel down the **accessory pathway**. Unlike the AV node, this pathway usually does not slow conduction at fast rates (no decremental conduction). The ventricular rate climbs and can trigger **ventricular fibrillation**. For this reason, **AV-nodal blocking agents** are avoided in pre-excited AF. Torsades de pointes is linked to a long QT, not to AV nodal blockade.
questions.explanation_pt: Trata-se de **FA pré-excitada** na **síndrome de Wolff-Parkinson-White**. Bloquear o **nó AV** elimina a via normal concorrente, então os impulsos atriais rápidos descem pela **via acessória**. Diferentemente do nó AV, essa via em geral não tem condução decremental. A frequência ventricular sobe e pode desencadear **FV**. Por isso, **bloqueadores do nó AV** são evitados na FA pré-excitada. A torsades de pointes está associada ao QT longo, e não ao bloqueio do nó AV.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after two episodes of fainting today. Pulse is 36/min and regular. Blood pressure is 102/58 mm Hg. Exam of the neck shows intermittent large "cannon" a waves. ECG shows regular P waves at 90/min and regular wide QRS complexes at 36/min. The PR interval varies from beat to beat, and no P wave has a fixed relation to a QRS complex. Which diagnosis is most likely?
choices: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type I
Second-degree AV block, Mobitz type II
questions.explanation: Atria and ventricles beat **independently** (**AV dissociation**): P waves and QRS complexes each have their own regular rate with no fixed PR. This is **third-degree AV block**, with a slow **ventricular escape rhythm** (wide QRS). **Cannon a waves** appear when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve. In Mobitz II, the PR of conducted beats is constant. Treatment is a **pacemaker**.
questions.explanation_pt: Átrios e ventrículos batem de forma **independente** (**dissociação AV**): ondas P e complexos QRS têm cada um sua própria frequência regular, sem PR fixo. Trata-se de **BAV de terceiro grau (BAV total)**, com **ritmo de escape ventricular** lento (QRS largo). As **ondas a em canhão** surgem quando o átrio contrai contra a valva tricúspide fechada. No Mobitz II, o PR dos batimentos conduzidos é constante. O tratamento é **marca-passo**.

notes.title: Arrhythmias: key rhythms and how to recognize them
notes.body_md:
## Supraventricular rhythms

- **Atrial fibrillation**: **irregularly irregular**, no P waves. Causes include hypertension, mitral valve disease, hyperthyroidism and alcohol. Thrombus in the **left atrial appendage** can cause stroke, so many patients need **anticoagulation**.
- **Atrial flutter**: **sawtooth waves**, atrial rate near 300/min, often 2:1 conduction. Reentry through the **cavotricuspid isthmus**.
- **AV nodal reentrant tachycardia**: regular, narrow-complex, sudden onset and end. Vagal maneuvers first, then **adenosine**.
- **Wolff-Parkinson-White**: **accessory pathway**, short PR, **delta wave**. In pre-excited AF, avoid **AV-nodal blocking agents**.

## AV blocks

- **First degree**: PR >200 ms, every P conducted; benign.
- **Mobitz I (Wenckebach)**: PR lengthens until a QRS drops; usually at the **AV node**.
- **Mobitz II**: constant PR, sudden dropped QRS; **below the AV node**; may progress, so pace.
- **Third degree**: **AV dissociation**, slow escape rhythm, cannon a waves; needs a **pacemaker**.

## Sinus node disease

- **Sick sinus syndrome**: usually age-related fibrosis of the sinus node. Sinus pauses, bradycardia, often alternating with atrial tachyarrhythmias (**tachy-brady syndrome**).

## Ventricular rhythms

- **Ventricular tachycardia**: monomorphic VT has wide, regular QRS complexes; often from scar after MI. Can cause collapse or degenerate into VF.
- **Ventricular fibrillation**: chaotic, no organized QRS, no pulse; needs immediate **defibrillation**.
- **Torsades de pointes**: polymorphic VT that twists around the baseline. It comes from a **long QT**.

## Long QT and channel disorders

- **Acquired**: QT-prolonging drugs (e.g., macrolides, some antipsychotics), **hypokalemia**, **hypomagnesemia**, hypocalcemia. Treat torsades with **IV magnesium**.
- **Congenital**: **Romano-Ward** (autosomal dominant) and **Jervell and Lange-Nielsen** (autosomal recessive, with **deafness**).
- **Brugada**: Na+ channel defect; pseudo-RBBB and ST elevation in V1-V3; risk of sudden death; **ICD**.
notes.body_pt_md:
## Ritmos supraventriculares

- **Fibrilação atrial (FA)**: **irregularmente irregular**, sem ondas P. Causas incluem hipertensão, valvopatia mitral, hipertireoidismo e álcool. Trombo no **apêndice atrial esquerdo** pode causar AVC, por isso muitos pacientes precisam de **anticoagulação**.
- **Flutter atrial**: **ondas em dente de serra**, frequência atrial perto de 300/min, muitas vezes condução 2:1. Reentrada pelo **istmo cavotricuspídeo**.
- **Taquicardia por reentrada nodal (TRN)**: regular, QRS estreito, início e término súbitos. Primeiro manobras vagais, depois **adenosina**.
- **Wolff-Parkinson-White**: **via acessória**, PR curto, **onda delta**. Na FA pré-excitada, evitar **bloqueadores do nó AV**.

## Bloqueios AV

- **BAV de primeiro grau**: PR >200 ms, toda P é conduzida; benigno.
- **Mobitz I (Wenckebach)**: o PR aumenta até um QRS falhar; geralmente no **nó AV**.
- **Mobitz II**: PR constante, falha súbita do QRS; **abaixo do nó AV**; pode progredir, então indica-se marca-passo.
- **BAV de terceiro grau (BAV total)**: **dissociação AV**, ritmo de escape lento, ondas a em canhão; exige **marca-passo**.

## Doença do nó sinusal

- **Síndrome do nó sinusal doente**: geralmente por fibrose do nó sinusal relacionada à idade. Pausas sinusais, bradicardia, muitas vezes alternando com taquiarritmias atriais (**síndrome bradicardia-taquicardia**, ou bradi-taqui).

## Ritmos ventriculares

- **Taquicardia ventricular (TV)**: a TV monomórfica tem QRS largo e regular; muitas vezes por cicatriz pós-IAM. Pode causar colapso ou degenerar em FV.
- **Fibrilação ventricular (FV)**: caótica, sem QRS organizado, sem pulso; exige **desfibrilação** imediata.
- **Torsades de pointes**: TV polimórfica que gira em torno da linha de base. Decorre de um **QT longo**.

## QT longo e canalopatias

- **Adquirido**: fármacos que prolongam o QT (ex.: macrolídeos, alguns antipsicóticos), **hipocalemia**, **hipomagnesemia**, hipocalcemia. Tratar a torsades com **magnésio IV**.
- **Congênito**: **Romano-Ward** (autossômica dominante) e **Jervell e Lange-Nielsen** (autossômica recessiva, com **surdez**).
- **Brugada**: defeito em canal de Na+; pseudobloqueio de ramo direito e supradesnivelamento do ST em V1-V3; risco de morte súbita; **CDI**.
